question: stage 51 showed throughput does not grow with asyncio concurrency after per-request CPU was cut, and blamed GIL-bound Python work. Does process-level parallelism help, and what breaks if it is used?

instrument.method: N independent processes, each with its own database connection and schema cache, sharing only the SQLite file on disk; a multiprocessing barrier starts them together and throughput is total attempts over the shared wall window (earliest start to latest finish), not the sum of per-worker durations
instrument.workload: the same in-process pipeline as scripts.scale_load (scripted router, no model call, execute against a seeded facts table)

results.reading: 4 processes give 3.2x at 1k tables and 3.1x at 10k tables, while stage 51 measured 1.0x for asyncio concurrency inside one process; per-request latency rises 18-32% as the processes share CPU and disk, which is the expected price and not a regression
results.statuses: every attempt reported ok at both scales, so the numbers are completed pipelines, not early failures

defect_found.what: two worker processes starting a workflow in the same microsecond produced the same trace file name, and the second writer failed with PermissionError on Windows
defect_found.cause: app/harness/runner.py built workflow_id as wf_{YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_%f} with no process or random component, and WorkflowTrace.persist() names the file after the id
defect_found.fix: _new_workflow_id() appends the pid; the id format used by the UI and audit is otherwise unchanged
defect_found.evidence: observed live in the first 1k run of the probe ('Workflow trace persistence failed ... PermissionError'), and reproduced by freezing the clock: same timestamp, different pid, different id

coverage: frozen clock plus two pids -> distinct ids, exact string asserted
throughput uses the shared window, so a late-starting worker cannot inflate it
pooled median and p95 over all workers
worker-count parsing rejects 0, negatives and empty input; the CLI returns 2 and writes nothing
the CLI refuses to reuse an existing fixture

blockers_for_real_deployment: schema cache is per process: N processes hold N copies (about 470 MB peak RSS each at 10k tables in the stage-51 measurement), so process count multiplies memory, not just CPU
the retrieval index directory (lancedb + sqlite bm25) was deliberately not built here; concurrent readers and a single writer across processes has not been accepted
the per-connection lease is an in-process object: N processes means N times the database connections, so the connection budget of the target database has to be recomputed
the admission gate (max_concurrent_queries) counts in one process, so the effective limit becomes N times the configured value
recovery and backup assume a single owner of the state directory: refresh_required markers and VACUUM INTO snapshots need a single writer
trace files are now collision-free by name, but there is no quota or cleanup policy for N processes writing into the same tree
usage audit appends were tested for concurrent threads, not for concurrent processes
corrections: stage 51 concluded that the remaining ceiling is GIL-bound CPU and that only moving work out of the process would help; this stage confirms the direction and quantifies it, but also shows the cost side (memory per process, connection budget, single-writer assumptions) that the earlier note did not name
not_covered: no HTTP transport: the workers call run_query in-process, so serialisation, connection acceptance and keep-alive costs are absent
no real model and no embedding provider; latency is orchestration time only
SQLite file reads only; PostgreSQL/MySQL behave differently under N connections
4 processes on a 24-core machine; no measurement above 4, and no test of CPU oversubscription
the probe does not run a server, so nothing here proves a deployment topology or an SLO

full_suite.note: both failures are the known Windows-only pair (hardlink alias CLI test, concurrent usage-audit writer); unchanged code paths

ci.conclusion: both workflows succeeded on the exact SHA; job logs still require admin rights
